merlin.name: 9 MERLIN ENGINES
merlin.fn: Nine kerosene/LOX engines in an octaweb: eight around one centre. Each gives ~845 kN at sea level and can throttle and relight for landing.

legs.name: LANDING LEGS
legs.fn: Four folding legs deploy seconds before touchdown and absorb the impact.

s1tank.name: STAGE 1 TANKS
s1tank.fn: LOX tank above the RP-1 tank, about 411 t of propellant in total; the common skin is the rocket's main structure.

interstage.name: INTERSTAGE
interstage.fn: Connects the two stages and covers the vacuum engine; pneumatic pushers separate the stages.

gridfins.name: GRID FINS
gridfins.fn: Four lattice fins steer the booster during descent like rudders.

mvac.name: VACUUM ENGINE
mvac.fn: One engine with a huge nozzle optimised for vacuum: ~981 kN.

s2tank.name: STAGE 2 TANKS
s2tank.fn: ~107 t of propellant to finish the climb to orbit.

capsule.name: CREW CAPSULE
capsule.fn: Capsule configuration: crew or cargo to the space station.

payload.name: PAYLOAD
payload.fn: The satellite being launched, mounted on an adapter.

fairing.name: FAIRING
fairing.fn: Two shells protect the payload through the atmosphere, then split apart.

raptors.name: 33 RAPTOR ENGINES
raptors.fn: Full-flow methane/LOX engines: 13 centre engines gimbal, 20 outer ones are fixed. ~74 MN together.

shTank.name: SUPER HEAVY TANKS
shTank.fn: About 3,400 t of liquid methane and oxygen in steel tanks.

gridfinsSH.name: SUPER HEAVY GRID FINS
gridfinsSH.fn: Steer the booster and act as lifting points for the tower catch.

hotRing.name: HOT-STAGING RING
hotRing.fn: Vented ring that lets the ship light its engines while still attached.

shipEngines.name: SHIP ENGINES
shipEngines.fn: 3 sea-level Raptors for landing and 3 vacuum Raptors for the climb to orbit.

shipTank.name: SHIP TANKS
shipTank.fn: ~1,500 t of propellant plus header tanks for the landing flip.

payloadBay.name: PAYLOAD BAY
payloadBay.fn: A 'Pez dispenser' slot releases Starlink satellites one by one.

heatshield.name: HEAT SHIELD
heatshield.fn: ~18,000 black hex tiles protect the belly from ~1,400 °C plasma.

flaps.name: FLAPS
flaps.fn: Two forward and two aft flaps steer the belly-flop, like a skydiver's arms and legs.

specs.cmpAria: Height comparison of Falcon 9 and Starship
specs.cgTitle: CG and CP: why don't real rockets have big tail fins?
specs.cgBody: A model rocket is stable when its centre of gravity (CG) sits above its centre of pressure (CP), usually by 1–2 body diameters, so fins are needed. Big rockets fly mostly above thick air and steer their engines (gimbal), so they stay controlled even with a small margin; the grid fins and flaps only work on the way back down. In this model the margin is negative: with no fins the CP sits above the CG, so the stack is aerodynamically unstable and engine gimbal keeps it pointed.

phases.title: Flight phases
phases.lead: From leaving the pad to the booster coming home.

f9.p: Nine engines at ~7.6 MN lift 549 t. The rocket rises vertically, then pitches slightly east.
Highest aerodynamic pressure. The engines throttle down briefly so the structure is not overloaded.
Stage 1 shuts down at ~70 km and ~8,000 km/h; the stages separate and the vacuum engine lights.
For a pad return the booster flips and burns back. For a drone ship it only flips and coasts on.
Three engines fire for ~20 s to slow from ~5,000 km/h, protecting the booster from heating.
One engine, legs out, about 2 m/s at touchdown on the drone ship or landing pad.
Stage 2 cuts off at ~27,000 km/h: the payload is in orbit.

ss.p: 33 Raptors, ~74 MN. Flight 11 lifted off on 13/10/2025 (US), 06:23 on 14/10 UTC+7.
The ship lights its 6 engines while still attached, pushing off through the vented ring.
Super Heavy flips, burns back, drops the ring and heads for the Gulf of Mexico.
13 then 5 engines slow the booster to a hover before it drops into the sea (or is caught by the tower).
The ship coasts and deploys 8 Starlink simulators through the payload door.
One engine is relit in space, rehearsing a deorbit burn.
Belly-first at ~26,000 km/h; plasma wraps the hex tiles while the flaps steer.
Engines relight, the ship swings vertical and splashes down in the Indian Ocean.

news.title: News · Starship Flight 11
news.lead: Summary of the article and related milestones.
news.headline: SpaceX launches the largest rocket in history into space
facts: On the night of 13/10 (US time), Starship, the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, launched from the southern tip of Texas.
This was the 11th test flight; the booster separated and headed into the Gulf of Mexico as planned.
The ship carried 8 Starlink simulator satellites and flew halfway around the world before splashing down in the Indian Ocean.
The whole flight lasted just over an hour, from the Starbase site near the Mexican border.
Tests over the Indian Ocean rehearse a future return to the launch site; the August flight had also succeeded on a similar route.
Starship is meant to take people to Mars, and nearer term to land NASA astronauts on the Moon later this decade.

timeline.p: Hot staging; Super Heavy boosts back towards the Gulf.
Booster landing burn and splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.
Ship splashes down in the Indian Ocean (~07:29 UTC+7).

safety.title: Notes & sources
safety.p1: An educational visualisation, not engineering data. Geometry is simplified, masses and timelines are public estimates, and the Falcon 9 trajectory comes from a simple 2-D model. No logos or trademarks are used.
